analysis.one_liner: Requires old grandfathered coal-fired power plants to meet modern Clean Air Act emission standards.
analysis.headline: The bill to close the loophole letting pre-1971 power plants skip modern pollution controls was referred to committee and never received a vote before Congress adjourned.
analysis.plain_summary: The Clean Air Act's pollution rules for power plants applied only to newer facilities, so thousands of older coal- and oil-fired units were "grandfathered" and allowed to keep polluting at much higher levels. This bill would have removed that exemption for large grandfathered plants whose electricity crosses state lines, requiring them to meet modern emission standards within five years. As an alternative way to comply, it would have set national emission limits starting in 2003 and let plants trade pollution allowances, similar to the system used for acid rain.
analysis.who_benefits: People who live downwind of old, heavily polluting power plants — especially in the Northeast, whose senators sponsored the bill — would breathe cleaner air, since the bill targets the oldest units that emit the most sulfur dioxide, nitrogen oxides, and other pollutants. Utilities that already invested in modern pollution controls would also gain, because the bill's own findings note they face an unfair competitive disadvantage against older plants that spend less on controls, particularly now that electricity markets are open to interstate competition. [S3]
analysis.who_benefits_short: People living downwind of old coal plants

how_it_helps.text: Ends the Clean Air Act 'grandfather' exemption so older electric utility units would have to meet the same emission standards as new plants — within five years for standards already on the books, and within three years of any standard adopted after enactment.

Covers the large plants that matter most: any fossil-fired unit over 25 megawatts whose electricity flows across state lines, closing a gap the bill says grew worse once utility deregulation let cheap, dirty old plants increase their generation and emissions.

Offers a flexible alternative compliance path: national emission caps starting in 2003, with transferable allowances allocated by generation share, so plants that cut pollution cheaply could sell allowances to others while the overall cap holds.
Leaves all other Clean Air Act obligations — health-based air quality standards and state implementation plans — fully intact, so the bill adds a requirement rather than weakening existing ones.

analysis.who_pays: Owners and operators of grandfathered coal- and oil-fired power plants, which would face the cost of installing modern emission controls or buying allowances under the national cap. Some of those costs could eventually show up in electricity prices in regions that depend on old coal plants, though the bill gives plants five years and a flexible trading option to soften the burden.
analysis.who_pays_short: Owners of grandfathered coal-fired power plants

drawbacks.text: Retrofitting or cleaning up decades-old plants is expensive, and some of those compliance costs could be passed through to electricity customers, particularly in coal-dependent states.

The alternative compliance path relies on an allowance-trading cap rather than requiring every plant to install controls, so some individual old plants could keep emitting at high levels in a given year simply by buying allowances, leaving local communities near those plants with less immediate relief than a strict unit-by-unit mandate.

analysis.benefit_vs_cost: The public health and environmental gain from forcing the oldest, dirtiest power plants to meet modern standards is large and well-documented in the bill's own findings, and the five-year deadline plus tradable allowances were designed to keep costs manageable. The honest trade-offs are real but modest: retrofit costs that could reach ratepayers and the possibility that allowance trading concentrates continued pollution around a few old plants. On balance the bill was a targeted, reasonably designed fix to a well-known loophole.

outcome.mechanism: It was introduced in the Senate in October 1998, sent to the Environment and Public Works Committee, and died there when Congress adjourned two months later without any hearing, vote, or further action.

narrative.text: Sen. Joseph Lieberman introduced the bill on October 9, 1998, joined by original cosponsors Sens. Dodd, Kerry, Lautenberg, and Torricelli, all Democrats from Northeastern states downwind of Midwest coal pollution.
Six senators cosponsored the bill — five Democrats and one Republican — giving it a small bipartisan base of support.
The Senate read the bill twice and referred it to the Committee on Environment and Public Works; that was the last action ever taken on it.
The 105th Congress ended on January 3, 1999, and the bill expired in committee without a hearing, a markup, or a floor vote.

outcome.who_came_out_ahead: Owners of grandfathered coal- and oil-fired power plants came out ahead: the loophole that let their old units avoid modern pollution controls stayed open, while downwind communities continued to bear the health costs of the extra emissions.

analysis.who_came_out_ahead_short: Owners of old coal-fired power plants

against.name: Coal-burning electric utilities
against.role: Owners and operators of grandfathered power plants
against.what_they_did: The industry that benefits from the grandfather exemption has a long public record of resisting efforts to close it, since modern controls on old plants would impose major compliance costs.

sides.party_line_note: The bill's sponsors were five Democrats plus one Republican, so its base was bipartisan, but with no votes ever held the partisan shape of the full Senate is unknown.

industries.industry: Coal- and oil-fired electric utilities with grandfathered plants
industries.note: These operators would have had to install modern emission controls or buy allowances under a national cap, a multibillion-dollar cost for units that had escaped such requirements since the 1970s. Their interest in keeping the exemption runs directly against the health of people breathing their emissions.

Stricter emissions standards on old coal-fired units make burning coal at those plants more expensive, which would reduce demand for coal over time. Cheaper pollution control alternatives and fuel switching are the competitive threat.

industries.industry: Utilities with newer, cleaner power plants
industries.note: The bill's findings state that utilities meeting strict environmental standards are unfairly disadvantaged in the new competitive electricity market by old plants that spend less on controls; leveling that playing field would help them. Their competitive gain coincides with cleaner air for the public.

The bill builds compliance for grandfathered units around transferable allowances under national caps starting in 2003, extending the market-based acid rain model to more pollutants and giving the trading system a bigger permanent role in air regulation.
